input.instructions: Create a compact, accurate blueprint for an 8-to-12-minute educational lesson with exactly ten sequential teaching beats. Do not write full narration. Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. For every beat, provide one distinct complete factual claim, a concrete example, a concise editable visual direction, and one or two exact supplied source IDs. End the claim, example, and visual direction with complete punctuation. Every cited source excerpt must directly support the claim; reuse at least two important technical terms from each cited excerpt so support can be checked locally. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Keep the claim, example, and visual direction compact; a deterministic local expander will produce the full narration. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Every factual claim must cite one or more supplied source IDs. Narration must describe information that is essential to understand visuals. Do not imitate a named creator or invent sources.
input.prompt:
Topic: CSCI-472: Historical & Current Perspectives in Computer Science. Create a representative course-foundations companion aligned to the official catalog description. It must teach durable concepts and problem-solving methods without claiming to replace the instructor's syllabus. Official catalog description: Students who have a background in Computer Science theories, algorithms, and data structures will be provided a look at the history of Computer Science from historical and current perspectives. Topics include an early history of Computer Science, a study of the people who shaped Computer Science, and a discussion of major milestones in Computer Science. Additionally, students will study current issues in Computer Science, including legal, ethical, diversity, equity, inclusion, accessibility and privacy issues, and how past issues affect modern designs and decision making by computer scientists. Students will be required to work in teams on several assignments. Papers, presentations, and oral presentations are required. Students cannot take and receive credit for this course if they have credit for CSCI-471. Prerequisites: This class is restricted to students with at least 4th year standing. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 It may be used to fulfill one of the following: Writing Intensive: Program Typically Offered: Fall or Spring or Summer

Source excerpts:

[nist-cryptographic-standards]
Cryptographic standards define approved algorithms and parameters. Encryption supports confidentiality when keys and modes are used correctly. Message authentication and digital signatures address integrity and authenticity in different ways. Random number generation supports keys, nonces, and other security parameters. Key management covers generation, distribution, storage, use, rotation, revocation, and destruction. Modes of operation define how a primitive processes data larger than one block. Validation checks implementations against specified requirements. Security depends on the complete protocol and implementation, not only an algorithm name. Analysis also considers side channels and migration requirements.

[nist-ssdf]
The Secure Software Development Framework groups practices into four practice groups. Prepare the Organization establishes people, processes, and technology for secure development. Protect the Software prevents unauthorized access to code and development artifacts. Produce Well-Secured Software addresses security requirements, design, verification, and release. Respond to Vulnerabilities identifies, analyzes, remediates, and learns from discovered weaknesses. Security requirements should be tracked throughout development. Verification provides evidence that selected practices and controls were performed. Security reasoning identifies assets, trust boundaries, threats, controls, evidence, residual risk, and responsibilities.

[rit-csci-472]
Students who have a background in Computer Science theories, algorithms, and data structures will be provided a look at the history of Computer Science from historical and current perspectives. Topics include an early history of Computer Science, a study of the people who shaped Computer Science, and a discussion of major milestones in Computer Science. Additionally, students will study current issues in Computer Science, including legal, ethical, diversity, equity, inclusion, accessibility and privacy issues, and how past issues affect modern designs and decision making by computer scientists. Students will be required to work in teams on several assignments. Papers, presentations, and oral presentations are required. Students cannot take and receive credit for this course if they have credit for CSCI-471. Prerequisites: This class is restricted to students with at least 4th year standing. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 It may be used to fulfill one of the following: Writing Intensive: Program Typically Offered: Fall or Spring or Summer

beats.title: Course Foundations & Prerequisites
beats.visualDirection: Display a course eligibility matrix highlighting the fourth-year requirement and the CSCI-471 exclusion rule.

beats.claim: The early history of computer science traces the evolution of computational concepts from ancient mathematical systems to modern algorithmic frameworks.
beats.example: Ancient Babylonian and Greek mathematical methods laid the groundwork for later algorithmic thinking in computing.
beats.title: Early History of Computer Science
beats.visualDirection: Show a timeline graphic connecting ancient mathematical practices to the development of modern algorithms.

beats.claim: The study of the people who shaped computer science highlights the contributions of diverse pioneers who advanced computational theory and practice.
beats.example: Historical figures like Ada Lovelace and Alan Turing are recognized for their foundational work in programming and theoretical computation.
beats.title: People Who Shaped Computer Science
beats.visualDirection: Present a portrait collage of key historical figures with brief annotations on their specific contributions.

beats.claim: A discussion of major milestones in computer science covers critical technological breakthroughs that transformed computing capabilities and applications.
beats.example: The invention of the transistor and the development of integrated circuits marked pivotal shifts in hardware architecture and processing power.
beats.title: Major Milestones in Computer Science
beats.visualDirection: Display a slide sequence showing key hardware and software milestones with dates and brief impact statements.

beats.claim: The Secure Software Development Framework groups practices into four practice groups: Prepare the Organization, Protect the Software, Produce Well-Secured Software, and Respond toV
beats.example: Prepare the Organization establishes people, processes, and technology for secure development, ensuring foundational readiness before coding begins.
beats.title: Secure Software Development Framework
beats.visualDirection: Show a four-quadrant diagram mapping each practice group to its core responsibilities and deliverables.

beats.claim: Cryptographic standards define approved algorithms and parameters that support confidentiality when keys and modes are used correctly.
beats.example: AES encryption standards specify block sizes and key lengths that ensure data remains unreadable without proper authentication.
beats.title: Cryptographic Standards & Confidentiality
beats.visualDirection: Display a comparison table of AES modes of operation showing how each processes data larger than one block.

beats.claim: Message authentication and digital signatures address integrity and authenticity in different ways, while key management covers generation, distribution, storage, use, rotation,rev
beats.example: Digital signatures verify the origin of a message, and key rotation policies ensure compromised keys are replaced before expiration.
beats.title: Integrity, Authenticity & Key Management
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate a key lifecycle flowchart showing generation, distribution, storage, use, rotation, and destruction steps.

beats.claim: Verification provides evidence that selected practices and controls were performed, while security reasoning identifies assets, trust boundaries, threats, controls, evidence, and a
beats.example: Security reasoning maps a web application's trust boundaries to identify where user input enters the system and where data is stored.
beats.title: Verification & Security Reasoning
beats.visualDirection: Show a trust boundary diagram highlighting assets, threats, and controls within a software architecture.

beats.claim: Students will study current issues in computer science, including legal, ethical, diversity, equity, inclusion, accessibility and privacy issues.
beats.example: Privacy regulations like GDPR require data minimization and user consent mechanisms in modern application design.
beats.title: Current Issues: Legal, Ethical & Privacy
beats.visualDirection: Display a checklist of current CS issues with icons representing legal, ethical, DEI, accessibility, and privacy domains.

beats.claim: Past issues affect modern designs and decision making by computer scientists, demonstrating how historical lessons inform current technical choices.
beats.example: Early vulnerabilities in cryptographic protocols led to modern side-channel attack mitigations and stricter validation checks in implementations.
beats.title: Past Issues Affecting Modern Design
beats.visualDirection: Show a cause-and-effect diagram linking historical security failures to contemporary design standards and validation practices.

learningObjectives: Define the four practice groups of the Secure Software Development Framework and explain their roles in software security.
Explain how cryptographic standards, key management, and modes of operation collectively support confidentiality, integrity, and authenticity.
Analyze how historical milestones and current legal, ethical, and privacy issues shape modern computer science design and decision-making.
